title: Quiz: System Architecture - Intermediate
prompt: Test your intermediate understanding of memory models, bus systems, and CPU instruction cycles.

questions.question: Which of the following describes a key characteristic of a von Neumann architecture compared to a Harvard architecture?
options: A von Neumann architecture uses a single accumulator.
In a von Neumann architecture, RAM contains both data and programs.
A von Neumann architecture is strictly for RISC machines.
A von Neumann architecture executes instructions in one cycle.
questions.explanation: In a von Neumann architecture, RAM contains both data and programs, whereas a Harvard architecture uses separate memories for data and programs.
questions.hint: Think about how memory is partitioned (or not partitioned) for storing instructions and variables.

questions.question: How do Load/Store machines differ from Accumulator machines when accessing RAM?
options: Only load and store instructions can access RAM, while other instructions operate on the register file.
Load/Store machines use the accumulator for all ALU results.
Load/Store machines perform operations directly in primary memory.
Load/Store machines bypass the control unit to transfer data.
questions.explanation: In a Load/Store machine, only load and store instructions can access RAM, and other instructions operate on a specified register file.
questions.hint: Consider the name 'Load/Store'—those are the only two actions allowed to interact directly with memory.

questions.question: What is a defining trait of machine instruction sizes in a RISC architecture?
options: They vary in length from 1 to 15 bytes to save memory.
They dynamically resize based on immediate data.
They are always the same size, making decoding simpler and faster.
They are always exactly one byte long.
questions.explanation: Machine instructions are always the same size in RISC architectures, which makes decoding simpler and faster.
questions.hint: ARMv8 instructions are an example of this architecture and are always 32 bits wide.

questions.question: What specific address does the Program Counter (PC) hold during execution?
options: The memory address of the ALU result.
The address in memory of the currently executing instruction.
The secondary memory address of the file system.
The memory-mapped I/O device address.
questions.explanation: The Program Counter (PC) contains the address in memory of the currently executing instruction, and it is incremented to execute the next instruction.
questions.hint: This register tracks where the CPU is currently 'looking' in the code.

questions.question: What is the purpose of pseudo-ops (assembler directives) in an assembly program?
options: They generate multi-cycle machine instructions for the ALU.
They execute loops and branch targets during runtime.
They do not generate machine instructions, but give the assembler extra information.
They dynamically allocate secondary memory.
questions.explanation: Pseudo-ops do not generate machine instructions, but give the assembler extra information, like defining globals.
questions.hint: Think of them as instructions for the translator (the assembler), not instructions for the CPU itself.

questions.question: What are the three sub-components of the system bus?
options: Input, Output, and Execution busses
Address, Data, and Control busses
Primary, Secondary, and Peripheral busses
ALU, CU, and Register busses
questions.explanation: The bus is often subdivided into the address, data, and control busses.
questions.hint: One specifies location, one transfers information, and one monitors devices.

questions.question: Where are ALU results always put in an Accumulator Machine architecture?
options: Into a destination register within the register file
Directly into primary memory
Into the Status Register (SR)
Into the accumulator register (ACC)
questions.explanation: In an Accumulator Machine, ALU results are always put into the ACC.
questions.hint: The name of the architecture is a big clue for where it forces all of its arithmetic outputs.

questions.question: Which register contains information (flags) about the result of a previous instruction, such as an overflow?
options: Instruction Register (IR)
Program Counter (PC)
Status Register (SR)
Control Unit (CU)
questions.explanation: The Status Register (SR) contains information (flags) about the result of a previous instruction.
questions.hint: It tracks the 'status' of the last calculation, like whether there was a carry bit.
